title: The COVID-19 Infodemic: A Quantitative Analysis Through Facebook
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 454 COVID-19-related Facebook posts, each cross-checked against WHO and CDC guidance and classified as correct information, misinformation, or unverifiable information. 146 posts were classified as misinformation, a share of items with a stated denominator, so this is a CONTENT estimate.

estimates.country: Not stated; English-language Facebook posts worldwide (authors based in Karachi, Pakistan)
estimates.measure_type: % of COVID-19-related Facebook posts classified as misinformation (content that could easily be rebutted using WHO or CDC guidance)
estimates.value_raw: 146 posts of 454. The paper PRINTS '146 posts (22.3%)', but 22.3% = 146/654, not 146/454; the study's own post total is 454, so the correct part/whole share is 146/454 = 32.2%. See notes for the arithmetic proof.
estimates.denominator: 454 English-language Facebook posts with at least 10 likes, returned by searches on 17 COVID-19 hashtags from a newly created account, 14-16 July 2020
estimates.definition: A post counted in the numerator if it 'included any content that could be easily be rebutted' using the updated WHO or CDC guidelines. The complementary categories were 'correct information' (corresponding to WHO/CDC guidance) and 'unverifiable information' (could not be proven either correct or incorrect by those sources).
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation is defined as a 'claim of fact that is currently false due to lack of scientific evidence'"
estimates.source_quote: In total, 146 posts (22.3%) included misinformation, 128 (19.6%) included unverifiable information and 180 (27.5%) include correct information verified by WHO or CDC
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Misinformation, correct, and unverifiable information', p. 4; also Abstract (Results)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: The authors themselves classified each post as correct / misinformation / unverifiable by cross-checking it against the updated WHO and CDC guidelines. The paper reports NO number of coders per post, no independent double-coding procedure, no adjudication rule and NO inter-rater reliability statistic of any kind.
estimates.moderator_quote: We used the Facebook search bar using multiple keywords, as mentioned in Figure 1. Our search was restricted to posts in the English language only and to those having a minimum of 10 likes. We eliminated posts that had less than 10 likes Data of all the posts in the results of the searched hashtag were collected that included any information relating to coronavirus
estimates.notes: MAJOR ARITHMETIC PROBLEM IN THE PAPER -- the adjudicator must decide between 22.3% (as printed) and 32.2% (146/454). Evidence that the denominator behind every printed percentage is 654, not the stated 454: 291/654=44.5%, 156/654=23.9%, 130/654=19.9%, 114/654=17.4%, 30/654=4.6%, 12/654=1.8%, 264/654=40.4%, 84/654=12.8%, 99/654=15.1%, 287/654=43.9%, 68/654=10.4%, 96/654=14.7%, 146/654=22.3%, 128/654=19.6%, 180/654=27.5% -- all fifteen headline percentages match /654 to the printed decimal, and none matches /454. Evidence that the true post total is nonetheless 454: (a) the text states 'Our study consists of a total of 454 Facebook posts'; (b) the three accuracy categories are exhaustive and sum exactly to it, 146+128+180=454; (c) Table 3's WITHIN-GROUP percentages are computed correctly and imply 291 verified + 163 unverified accounts = 454 posts (80/291=27.5%, 66/163=40.5%, 126/291=43.3%, 54/163=33.1%, 85/291=29.2%, 43/163=26.4%, and 80+66=146, 126+54=180, 85+43=128). So the count 146 and the denominator 454 are both well supported, while the printed 22.3% is computed on a phantom denominator. I therefore report the R8-permitted exact part/whole share 146/454 = 32.2%, with the printed figure preserved verbatim in value_raw and source_quote. confidence=medium solely because of this discrepancy; the classification itself is straightforward.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted, with reasons: (1) 'Unverifiable information', 128 posts (printed 19.6%; 128/454 = 28.2%). Defined as posts that 'could not be proven either correct or incorrect' against WHO/CDC -- an absence of verification, not a falsity classification, so out of scope as a misinformation prevalence. It could be read as the upper bound of a broader definition (misinformation + unverifiable = 274/454 = 60.4%), but that is a cross-category sum I would have to compute, which R8 forbids. (2) Misinformation by ACCOUNT TYPE (Table 3, within-group shares): informal individual/group 65 (40.1%), healthcare/public health 51 (38.3%), NGO 8 (28.6%), news outlet/journalist 19 (16.5%), government 3 (printed '80.8%', clearly garbled -- the paired 'No' cell reads 13 (81.2%), so the intended value is 3/16 = 18.8%); verified accounts 80 (27.5%) vs unverified 66 (40.5%). These are source-type subgroups, not the paper's headline prevalence. (3) Misinformation rate BY HASHTAG lives in Figure 3, whose values are not in the extracted text; the Discussion quotes only '#vaccinedevelopment... a higher rate of misinformation (45.2%) and unverifiable information (28.7%)', a single-hashtag subgroup whose denominator is not stated anywhere. (4) Tone and topic distributions (serious 40.4%, humorous 12.8%, opinion 15.1%; public health 43.9%, socio-political 14.7%, financial 10.4%) are composition, not veracity; note they are also computed on the /654 denominator and do not sum to 100%. (5) The Twitter comparison figures quoted in the Discussion (Kouzy et al.) are cited from elsewhere -- excluded by R8. (6) The ABSTRACT states 'Most (22.5%) were posted by verified accounts', contradicting the Results' '291, 44.5%'; another symptom of the same numerical unreliability.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of Facebook, web-based search 14-16 July 2020 (three days). A newly created account was used to eliminate personalisation bias. Sampling frame: the Facebook search bar queried with 17 COVID-19 hashtags (listed in Figure 1); all posts returned that contained coronavirus-related information were collected; restricted to English and to posts with at least 10 likes (posts with fewer were eliminated). n=454 posts. Classification: each post categorised as correct information, misinformation or unverifiable information by cross-checking against updated WHO and CDC guidance. NO coder count, coding procedure, blinding or inter-rater reliability is reported -- the weakest point of the study alongside the arithmetic. Descriptive statistics and chi-square tests in SPSS 26, alpha 0.05. No IRB approval needed (public accounts). Authors' own limitations: English-language only; hashtag-based retrieval misses untagged COVID-19 posts; the three-day window may not capture changing topics.
rob.item6_quote: Posts that included any content that could be easily be rebutted using any of the aforementioned sites were considered misinformation while we categorized unverifiable information as posts that could not be proven either correct or incorrect by the same sources.
rob.item10_quote: In total, 146 posts (22.3%) included misinformation, 128 (19.6%) included unverifiable information and 180 (27.5%) include correct information verified by WHO or CDC (Figure 2).
